issues.legal_issue: The statutory vesting of private forest land as part of agrarian reform is within the legislative field for land reform and is constitutionally valid.
material_facts: The legislation was enacted to abolish intermediary interests and implement land reforms.
An amendment brought private forests within the statutory vesting scheme and vested the interests of forest owners in the State.
The statutory scheme provided for forests vested in the State to be managed by village bodies or other local authorities for the benefit of village communities.
issues.conclusion: The forest-vesting provision is part of agrarian reform and is valid; the management rule applies to forest land vested in the State.
issues.legal_principle: The legislation is, in pith and substance, about land and agrarian reform under Entry 18 of List II read with Entry 42 of List III of the Seventh Schedule. Incidental effect on forests does not invalidate it. Rule 41 provides for management of property vested in the State and applies to forest land as well. In Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab, the Court recognized that assigning land to village bodies for community use and rural welfare can be an essential part of agrarian reform.

predicates.challenge_to_agrarian_reform_acquisition: A party challenges the validity of a statutory acquisition of land carried out as part of an agrarian reform scheme.
predicates.acquisition_forms_part_of_land_reform: The statutory acquisition is part of a scheme to reform land tenure and abolish intermediary interests.
predicates.forest_management_is_assigned_to_village: The scheme provides for forests vested in the State to be managed by a village body or local authority for community benefit.

issues.definition: When a challenged acquisition forms part of land reform and provides for community management of the acquired forest, the acquisition is treated as valid.

issues.legal_issue: A State law directed principally to agrarian reform is not repugnant to a central law directed principally to forest management where the laws concern different subjects and can operate together.
material_facts: The State legislation principally addressed land tenure and agrarian reform, including the vesting of private forest land as land.
The central legislation principally addressed forests, including their management, preservation, transit, and forest produce.
The central legislation permitted acquisition for its purposes but did not require that all forest acquisitions occur under that process.
The two statutory schemes did not impose irreconcilable obligations or occupy the same field in their dominant purpose.
issues.conclusion: There is no repugnancy between the two laws, and no presidential assent was required to sustain the State law on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 254, repugnancy requires laws on a concurrent subject to occupy the same field and to conflict directly and irreconcilably, such that both cannot operate together; a central law intended as an exhaustive code may also exclude a State law. The Court applies the pith-and-substance doctrine and the triple test in M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India. It also relies on Hoechst Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. State of Bihar, Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab, Govt. of A.P. v. J.B. Educational Society, and State of Maharashtra v. Bharat Shanti Lal Shah. Incidental overlap between laws with different dominant purposes does not establish repugnancy.

rule.if: repugnancy_challenge_to_state_law and state_law_targets_land_reform and central_law_targets_forest_management and laws_can_operate_together

predicates.repugnancy_challenge_to_state_law: A party challenges a State law on the ground that it conflicts with a central law.
predicates.state_law_targets_land_reform: The State law principally concerns land tenure and agrarian reform.
predicates.central_law_targets_forest_management: The central law principally concerns forest management, preservation, or forest produce.
predicates.laws_can_operate_together: The two laws can operate without a direct, irreconcilable conflict or one law requiring disobedience of the other.

issues.definition: When the challenged State law principally concerns land reform, the central law principally concerns forest management, and both can operate together, the State law is not repugnant.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation for acquired private forest land cannot be denied merely because the forest owner derived no actual income from preserving the forest; its potential income must be considered.
material_facts: The owners’ private forest land vested in the State under the statutory scheme.
The owners stated that they had derived no income from the forest and had preserved it rather than exploiting it.
The statutory compensation formula referred to average annual income and provided compensation for private forests by reference to that income.
The forest was a productive asset, and potential income could be estimated by reference to comparable forests or by estimating income the property could have produced if exploited.
issues.conclusion: The owners are entitled to compensation; the authority must assess compensation using a reasonable and intelligible criterion that accounts for possible income, rather than awarding nothing because no actual income was earned.
issues.legal_principle: Article 300A permits deprivation of property only by authority of law. Compensation need not equal market value, and its adequacy is generally not reviewable, but compensation cannot be illusory or wholly absent. Sections 12, 18(1)(cc), and 19(1)(b), read with Section 4A of the applicable land-reform legislation, provide for compensation for vested private forests and require the statutory formula to be applied. Ganga Devi v. State of U.P., which construed actual income in its particular circumstances, did not concern a preserved, unexploited forest with possible income and was distinguishable. The Court distinguishes a potentially justifiable nil amount from no compensation at all.

rule.if: compensation_claim_after_statutory_taking and acquired_asset_is_private_forest and forest_was_preserved_without_realized_income and asset_had_potential_productivity

predicates.compensation_claim_after_statutory_takin: An owner seeks compensation after the State takes the owner’s property under a statutory scheme.
predicates.acquired_asset_is_private_forest: The property taken is a privately owned forest.
predicates.forest_was_preserved_without_realized_in: The owner preserved the forest and derived no actual income from it.
predicates.asset_had_potential_productivity: The forest could have produced income if exploited, or its possible income can be estimated using comparable property.

issues.definition: When a preserved private forest is taken, the absence of realized income does not permit compensation to be denied if the forest had potential productivity.

issues.legal_issue: Interest on compensation for acquired property runs from the date the owner is physically dispossessed, rather than automatically from the statutory vesting date.
material_facts: The Court directed that interest accompany the compensation award if the State had formally taken physical possession and the owner had been wholly deprived of possession.
The Court specified that if physical possession was handed over after statutory vesting, interest would run from the later handover date.
issues.conclusion: Interest is payable from the date of actual physical handover and total deprivation of possession; if possession was not handed over until later, interest starts on that later date.
issues.legal_principle: The Court’s direction ties interest on the compensation award to actual physical dispossession. Statutory vesting alone does not start interest where the owner has not yet handed over physical possession or has not been wholly deprived of it.

predicates.compensation_awarded_after_property_acqu: A compensation award is made following the State’s acquisition of property.
predicates.physical_handover_occurred: The owner actually handed over physical possession of the property to the State.
predicates.owner_was_wholly_deprived_of_possession: The owner was entirely deprived of physical possession of the property.

issues.definition: When compensation is awarded after acquisition and the owner actually hands over possession and is wholly deprived of it, interest runs from that handover.
